# How to Read This Book {.unnumbered}

***Subject 5 of 9 of the theoretical examination for the Sailplane Pilot Licence (SPL)***

There is nothing mysterious about a sailplane's aerodynamics. Only physics. And physics does not negotiate.

When the angle of attack exceeds the critical value, lift collapses, whatever the altitude. When the centre of gravity is beyond its aft limit, recovery from a spin may be impossible. When a spiral dive begins without outside references, the airspeed can pass V~NE~ before the pilot understands what is happening.

Seven chapters turn the physics of flight into real flying judgement: lift, drag, stability, control, the stall, the spin and the spiral dive.

The sailplane does not fly by magic. It flies because someone understood the physics before getting into the cockpit.

**Start at the end of each chapter**

Every chapter closes with a summary on a yellow background. It is not decoration, and it is not an afterthought. It is the chapter boiled down to what you must not forget.

Read it **before** you study the chapter, so that you know where you are heading, and come back to it **when you finish**, to check whether what you remember is what matters. On the eve of the exam, those summaries are your complete revision: if a single one feels unfamiliar, you know which chapter to reread.

**The boxes are not side notes**

The running text explains. The boxes warn, and each one speaks with a different voice. Once you recognise the voice, you know how to read the box:

::: {.callout-warning title="Safety"}
These flag anything that could cost you the glider, or your life, if you ignore it. Reread them before you fly, not before the exam.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Regulation"}
These set out what the law requires. There is no room for personal judgement: you comply. When they clash with your habits, it is the habit that is wrong.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Golden rule"}
These put into one sentence something that took a pilot years to learn, so that it takes you a minute.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Airmanship"}
These cover the judgement no regulation writes down: what separates a legal pilot from a good one. The regulations set the minimum; airmanship sets the standard.
:::

**How to find what you are looking for**

The **table of contents** in the front matter takes you to every chapter and its sections. After it comes the **list of figures**: the drawings and diagrams are numbered and referred to from the text, so you can go straight to the figure and back.

The **glossary**, at the end of the book, defines the terms and acronyms of the subject. Use it freely: much of the difficulty of aviation lies in its vocabulary, not in its ideas. The **bibliography** tells you where everything comes from and where to go next if a chapter leaves you wanting more.

**What this book is not**

This manual prepares you for the theoretical examination; it does not replace your instructor. Theory gives you judgement; judgement becomes piloting in the glider's seat, with an FI(S) beside you.

And when the regulations change, as they will, the legal text published by AESA or EASA takes precedence over anything you read here.
